title: From Cottage To Factory: Work Reorganised
text:
The most visible change in early industrial Britain was not the machine itself but where people worked and how their time was measured. Before mechanisation, a great deal of manufacturing happened in the home. A merchant supplied raw material to a household, collected the finished goods and paid by the piece. Families set their own hours, worked intensively before a delivery was due, rested afterwards, and combined the work with farming and childcare.

Powered machinery ended that arrangement, for a reason often misunderstood. It was not simply that engines were too large for a cottage. It was that expensive equipment had to be kept running, and keeping it running meant bringing workers to it on a schedule set by the owner. Payment shifted from the piece towards the hour, and timekeeping became a matter of discipline, enforced by gates, fines and clocks. The consequences ran through everything else. Homes stopped being workshops, so work and family life separated physically. Skill was redefined, as some crafts were broken into simpler repeated tasks while new trades in building and maintaining machinery appeared. Resistance followed, and it was not blind hostility to technology, as the caricature has it, but a defence of customary pay and control over one's own time.
points: Before mechanisation much manufacturing was done at home, with merchants supplying materials and paying by the piece.
Households controlled their own hours and combined the work with farming and family life.
Factories arose because costly machinery had to be kept running, which meant workers came to it on the owner's schedule.
Payment moved from piece rates to hourly work, and timekeeping was enforced by gates, fines and clocks.
Work and home separated, and skills were redefined as tasks were subdivided and new machine trades appeared.
Worker resistance was a defence of customary pay and control of time, not simple hostility to machines.
